lesson.menu_desc: Reading: the distance between what a court held and what the report says -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- A Judgment in Plain English
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 8 -- A Judgment in Plain English

paras: A court decision and the report of that decision are two different documents, and the distance between them is where most misunderstanding about the law lives. The judgment is long, hedged and written for other lawyers. The report is four hundred words, written the same afternoon, for people who will never read the original. The reporter is not being careless. She is doing something genuinely difficult: taking ninety pages in which a court held one narrow thing and said a great many others, and deciding which sentence was the decision.

The commonest error is a grammatical one with legal consequences. A report says that the court ruled that companies no longer have to do X. Read the judgment and you find something narrower: the court held that this agency, on this record, had not shown that it could require X of this company. It did not say that nobody has to. It did not even say the requirement was wrong. Reported speech is where that difference is either kept or quietly thrown away, because the verb you choose to report with carries a claim of its own. A court that noted something has done less than a court that held it, and a court that held it has done less than a court that struck down the rule.

There is also the question of who said it. Almost every important decision has a dissent, and the dissent is often the better writing: shorter, angrier and quotable. A reader who is skimming will remember the sentence that was quoted and not the label attached to it, so a line from a judge who LOST the argument can end up being described, six months later, as what the court decided. If a decision was unanimous, that is worth saying, because it is unusual and it tells you something. If it was not, saying so is not a detail.

So the discipline is simple and unglamorous. Name who held what. Keep the verb the court used, or a weaker one, and never a stronger one. Say what the decision does NOT decide, because the reader will assume it decides everything. And keep the sentence about the facts of that case, because the next case will have different ones. A summary that survives contact with the actual judgment is worth more than one that is exciting, and it is the only kind anybody will trust you for twice.

listenings.text: The first thing I do is not read the judgment. I read the last three pages, because that is where the court tells you what it actually decided, and everything before it is the argument for it. Then I go looking for one sentence: the one that would change if the case had come out the other way. That sentence is the decision. Everything else, however quotable, is either background or somebody being interesting. The mistake I made for years was quoting the best line I found, and the best line is very often in the dissent, because dissents are written to be read and majority opinions are written to be survived. Now I write the label first. The court held. Two judges disagreed. This does not decide the wider question. If those three sentences are true, I can make the rest as readable as I like.

I give every junior who joins us one rule about reporting a decision, and it is not about research. Never report with a stronger verb than the court used. If the judgment says the court noted something, you write noted. If it observed, you write observed. The temptation is enormous, because a memo that says the court held is more useful to the person reading it than a memo that says the court noted, and for about a week nobody finds out. Then somebody relies on your sentence in front of a client, or worse, in front of another court, and the whole thing comes back to the paragraph where you upgraded a verb. I have seen it happen twice. Both times the person was excellent and simply wanted to be helpful. Being helpful is what the rule is there to protect you from.

extra_audio.text: The judgment is handed down and runs to ninety pages. The last pages are read first, because that is where the court says what it decided. One sentence is identified: the one that would change if the case had gone the other way. The dissent is labelled as a dissent, so that nobody quotes it as the decision. And the summary is written with the verb the court used, and never a stronger one.
